summary: The bill lets college athletes sign name-image-likeness deals and earn other compensation up to a revenue-based cap set by athletic associations, bars improper payments from boosters or schools, requires high-revenue schools to keep at least 16 teams plus academic, medical, and degree-completion support, shields associations from antitrust suits for their rules, and overrides conflicting state laws.

scores.thoughts: The bill contains no provisions authorizing, expanding, or reducing any federal appropriations, grants, or expenditures. It regulates private and institutional conduct in college athletics without fiscal impact on the federal budget.
No tax rates, deductions, credits, or revenue provisions are addressed or altered.

Section 5 requires certain high-revenue institutions to furnish medical care, mental-health services, and insurance for student-athlete injuries. This is narrowly targeted at athletic programs and does not alter broader public versus private healthcare policy.
The bill has no provisions related to firearms, background checks, or gun regulations.
No immigration, visa, or border-related language appears.
No references to reproductive rights or abortion access.
No defense or military spending provisions exist.
No environmental, regulatory, or climate provisions are present.
The bill does not modify welfare, SNAP, Medicaid eligibility, or other safety-net programs.

The bill amends the Higher Education Act for athletic-fee transparency and imposes academic-support, degree-completion, and minimum-sport requirements on certain institutions. These changes are narrowly athletic and do not shift overall federal involvement versus privatization in K-12 or higher education policy.
Mentions of substance-abuse education appear only as one required life-skills topic; no decriminalization or enforcement changes are made.
No sentencing, policing, or criminal-justice reforms are included.
No tariffs, trade agreements, or protectionist measures appear.
No deficit, debt-ceiling, or fiscal-balance provisions exist.
No provisions address LGBTQ protections or restrictions.
No foreign-aid authorizations or reductions are present.
No voting-access or election-integrity measures are included.
Section 3(c) protects the privacy of NIL agreements by prohibiting release without consent. This is a narrow, ancillary privacy rule with minimal regulatory impact on technology or data policy.

Section 8 explicitly states that student athletes shall not be considered employees of institutions, conferences, or athletic associations based on participation. This directly precludes collective-bargaining or union rights for athletes and therefore strongly favors employer flexibility over worker/union protections.
No religious-exemption or civil-rights provisions are present.
